misconception

miss-kun-SEP-shun -- four syllables, stress on the third syllable, SEP. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Misconception is a mistaken belief about how something actually is.

It is a common misconception that goldfish have three-second memories.

Example

Half the class is certain that heavier objects fall faster. Nobody invented the misconception on purpose -- it simply feels obviously true, right up until two balls of different weights strike the floor at the same instant.

A misconception is an incorrect view produced by faulty thinking rather than by lying. It is honest and often widely shared, which is exactly what makes it so hard to shake.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

error: An error is any mistaken idea, judgment, or move -- one wrong answer, one bad call, quickly made and often quickly fixed. A misconception is a settled error about how something actually works, the kind a person carries around for years without noticing.

fallacy: A fallacy is a broken step in reasoning -- treating 'B came after A' as proof that A caused B. A misconception is the mistaken belief itself: a fallacy is how the thinking goes wrong; a misconception is the wrong idea you end up believing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fact: something known to be true

reality: the way things actually are

Where it sits · how settled and widely shared it is

misunderstanding → misconception → myth

misunderstanding vs. misconception: A misunderstanding is usually private and temporary -- you misheard the room number -- while a misconception is a settled wrong idea about how something works.

myth vs. misconception: Myth is a misconception that has gone public: one student's misconception stays inside one head, but a myth is repeated so often that everyone assumes it must be true.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — mis-: wrongly, badly (Old English)

prefix — con-: together (Latin)

root — cept-: to take, to grasp (Latin capere)

suffix — -ion: the act or result of (Latin -ionem)

Put it together: Misconception is mis- ('wrongly') added to conception, from Latin concipere -- con- ('together') plus capere ('to take, to grasp'). To conceive an idea is to grasp it; a misconception is an idea you have grasped in the wrong way and then carried around as if it were right.

Use the root in a new word: capture: The photographer waited two hours to capture the heron in flight.

Word Building

Word Choice

Misconception describes a wrong idea, not a lie: 'a common misconception,' 'clear up a misconception,' 'the misconception that spiders are insects.' The person holding it is mistaken, not dishonest. Someone who spreads a false idea on purpose is deceiving people -- a different charge entirely.
